subtopics.title: Energy bands and the classification of solids
subtopics.theory_md:
In a crystal the energy levels of the atoms broaden into **bands**. The **valence band** (VB) is the highest filled band, the **conduction band** (CB) lies above it, and the gap between them is the **forbidden gap** $E_g$.

- **Metal**: bands overlap or the CB is partly filled, so free electrons are always available.
- **Insulator**: VB full, CB empty, $E_g > 3$ eV (diamond 5.4 eV).
- **Semiconductor**: same picture with a small gap: Ge 0.7 eV, Si 1.1 eV.

At $T=0$ K a semiconductor has a full VB and an empty CB, so it is an insulator. As $T$ rises, electrons jump to the CB leaving **holes** in the VB; conductivity rises with $T$ (a metal's falls). **Intrinsic** = pure; **extrinsic** = doped (donors give n-type, acceptors give p-type).
subtopics.basics_md: Electrons in a full band are like people in a packed lift: nobody can move because there is no empty space. Free a few places (excite electrons across the gap) and movement becomes possible.
key_points: Bands: VB, CB, forbidden gap $E_g$ (Ge 0.7 eV, Si 1.1 eV)
Metal: overlapping or partly filled band; insulator: large gap; semiconductor: small gap
At 0 K a semiconductor has a full VB and empty CB, so it does not conduct
Conductivity of a semiconductor rises with temperature

subtopics.title: Fermi-Dirac function and Fermi energy
subtopics.theory_md:
The probability that a state of energy $E$ is occupied is
$$f(E)=\frac{1}{1+e^{(E-E_F)/k_BT}}$$
- $T=0$: a **step**, $f=1$ for $E<E_F$ and $f=0$ for $E>E_F$.
- $T>0$: the step is rounded over about $k_BT$ around $E_F$; **$f(E_F)=\tfrac12$ at every $T$**. Higher $T$ means more smearing.
- For $E-E_F\gg k_BT$: $f\approx e^{-(E-E_F)/k_BT}$.

**Fermi energy** $E_F$: the energy of the highest occupied state at $T=0$ K (the level where $f=\tfrac12$ at any $T$). For free electrons $E_F=\frac{h^2}{8m}\left(\frac{3n}{\pi}\right)^{2/3}$.

Numericals: $k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}$ eV/K, so $k_BT=0.0259$ eV at 300 K. Solve $\frac{E-E_F}{k_BT}=\ln\!\left(\frac1f-1\right)$.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of seats filling up from the front row at 0 K. Warming lets some people near the boundary row stand up and take a back seat, so the sharp edge blurs.
key_points: At 0 K a step at $E_F$; at $T>0$ rounded, with $f(E_F)=\frac12$

subtopics.title: Carrier concentration in an intrinsic semiconductor
subtopics.theory_md:
For $E-E_F\gg k_BT$ the FD function reduces to $e^{-(E-E_F)/kT}$. With density of states $g(E)=\frac{4\pi}{h^3}(2m_e^*)^{3/2}\sqrt{E-E_c}$:
$$n=\int_{E_c}^{\infty}g(E)f(E)\,dE=N_c\,e^{-(E_c-E_F)/kT},\quad N_c=2\left(\frac{2\pi m_e^*kT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}$$
using $\int_0^\infty x^{1/2}e^{-x/kT}dx=\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}(kT)^{3/2}$. Similarly $p=N_v\,e^{-(E_F-E_v)/kT}$ with $m_h^*$.

Intrinsic: $n=p=n_i$, so
$$n_i=\sqrt{N_cN_v}\,e^{-E_g/2kT}=2\left(\frac{2\pi kT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}(m_e^*m_h^*)^{3/4}e^{-E_g/2kT}$$
$n_i$ rises steeply with $T$ and falls with $E_g$. Numerically take $m^*=m=9.109\times10^{-31}$ kg unless told otherwise.
subtopics.basics_md: The number of electrons in the CB is (number of available states) times (probability each is filled). The probability is tiny and drops exponentially with the gap, which is why only a trickle of carriers exists.
key_points: Numericals: compute $kT$ in joules, then $N_c$, then the exponential

questions.q: Derive the expression for the concentration of electrons in the conduction band of an intrinsic semiconductor.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Step 1: density of states.** Electrons in the CB: $g(E)\,dE=\dfrac{4\pi}{h^3}(2m_e^*)^{3/2}(E-E_c)^{1/2}dE$.

**Step 2: occupation.** For $E-E_F\gg kT$: $f(E)\approx e^{-(E-E_F)/kT}$.

**Step 3: integrate.**
$$n=\frac{4\pi(2m_e^*)^{3/2}}{h^3}e^{-(E_c-E_F)/kT}\int_0^\infty x^{1/2}e^{-x/kT}dx,\ x=E-E_c$$
With the integral $=\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}(kT)^{3/2}$:
$$n=2\left(\frac{2\pi m_e^*kT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}e^{-(E_c-E_F)/kT}=N_ce^{-(E_c-E_F)/kT}$$
**Step 4:** with $E_F\approx(E_c+E_v)/2$, $n=p=n_i\propto e^{-E_g/2kT}$.

subtopics.title: Fermi level in an intrinsic semiconductor
subtopics.theory_md:
Set $n=p$ for the intrinsic crystal:
$$(m_e^*)^{3/2}e^{-(E_c-E_F)/kT}=(m_h^*)^{3/2}e^{-(E_F-E_v)/kT}$$
Take logs and solve:
$$\boxed{E_F=\frac{E_c+E_v}{2}+\frac{3kT}{4}\ln\frac{m_h^*}{m_e^*}}$$
- If $m_h^*=m_e^*$, or at $T=0$ K, $E_F=\frac{E_c+E_v}{2}$: **exactly mid-gap**.
- If $m_h^*\ne m_e^*$ the shift is linear in $T$ and only a few hundredths of an eV, far less than $E_g/2$, so $E_F$ always lies in the forbidden gap near its middle.
- Because $m_h^*>m_e^*$ usually, $E_F$ rises slightly with $T$.
subtopics.basics_md: Equal numbers of electrons and holes means the level that splits the two populations evenly sits in the middle of the gap. Unequal effective masses tilt it a little.
key_points: Temperature effect: small linear shift, stays in the gap

$\ln1.5=0.4055$, so shift $=0.75\times0.02585\times0.4055=7.9\times10^{-3}$ eV.

This is about 8 meV above mid-gap, tiny against $E_g/2=0.55$ eV.

$E_F$: highest occupied level at 0 K; $f=\frac12$ at any $T$

subtopics.title: Doped semiconductors: Fermi level and mass action
subtopics.theory_md:
**n-type**: donors (group V: P, As) add a level $E_d$ just below $E_c$; $n\approx N_D$ (majority electrons).
**p-type**: acceptors (group III: B, Al) add a level $E_a$ just above $E_v$; $p\approx N_A$.

**Law of mass action**: $np=n_i^2$ at a given $T$, so minority carriers $p=n_i^2/n$.

Fermi level: $E_F=E_i+kT\ln(n/n_i)$ for n-type, $E_F=E_i-kT\ln(p/n_i)$ for p-type. So $E_F$ moves **towards the CB for n-type** and **towards the VB for p-type**; at 0 K it lies midway between $E_d$ and $E_c$ (n) or $E_v$ and $E_a$ (p). At high $T$ the crystal turns intrinsic again and $E_F$ returns to mid-gap.
subtopics.basics_md: Doping adds many of one kind of carrier, so the level that balances electrons against holes must move towards the side with more carriers.
key_points: Donor level just below CB (n-type), acceptor level just above VB (p-type)
$E_F$ shifts toward CB in n-type and toward VB in p-type
At high temperature the extrinsic crystal becomes intrinsic

subtopics.title: Drift velocity and mobility
subtopics.theory_md:
Under a field $E$ carriers drift with **drift velocity** $v_d=\mu E$. The **mobility** $\mu=v_d/E=\dfrac{q\tau}{m^*}$ is the drift velocity per unit field; unit m$^2$/V s ($1\ \mathrm{m^2/Vs}=10^4\ \mathrm{cm^2/Vs}$).

Current density $J=nqv_d=nq\mu E$.

Typical values (m$^2$/V s): Ge $\mu_e=0.39$, $\mu_h=0.19$; Si $\mu_e=0.135$, $\mu_h=0.048$. Electrons are more mobile than holes (smaller effective mass). Mobility **falls** with temperature (lattice scattering, $\mu\propto T^{-3/2}$) and with doping (impurity scattering).
subtopics.basics_md: A carrier is pushed by the field but keeps bumping into the lattice, so it settles at a steady average speed. Mobility says how quickly that average speed grows with the push.
key_points: Mobility decreases with temperature and doping (scattering)

subtopics.title: Conductivity and resistivity of semiconductors
subtopics.theory_md:
Total conductivity: $\sigma=q(n\mu_e+p\mu_h)$, and $\rho=1/\sigma$.
- Intrinsic: $n=p=n_i$, $\sigma=n_iq(\mu_e+\mu_h)$.
- n-type: $\sigma\approx N_Dq\mu_e$. p-type: $\sigma\approx N_Aq\mu_h$ (the minority term is negligible since $p\ll n$ or $n\ll p$).

**Convert units first**: cm$^{-3}$ to m$^{-3}$ is $\times10^6$; cm$^2$/Vs to m$^2$/Vs is $\times10^{-4}$. Resistivity: $\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}=10^{-2}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{m}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Every free charge adds to the current. So conductivity is just (charge) times (how many) times (how easily each moves), added for electrons and holes.
key_points: Check units: cm to m conversions, unit of $\rho$

subtopics.title: Diffusion current and the Einstein relation
subtopics.theory_md:
Carriers also move by **diffusion** from high to low concentration. Diffusion current density (electrons): $J_n=qD_n\dfrac{dn}{dx}$; holes: $J_p=-qD_p\dfrac{dp}{dx}$, with $D$ the diffusion coefficient (m$^2$/s).

**Einstein relation** connecting the two transport processes:
$$\frac{D}{\mu}=\frac{k_BT}{q}$$
At 300 K $k_BT/q=0.0259$ V (the **thermal voltage**). Total current in a semiconductor = drift + diffusion.
subtopics.basics_md: Drift is a push by a field; diffusion is a spreading out from a crowded region. Both are caused by random thermal motion, so $D$ and $\mu$ are tied together by temperature.

subtopics.title: Hall effect: derivation, sign and applications
subtopics.theory_md:
A current $I$ along $x$ in a slab, with field $B$ along $z$ (perpendicular to $I$): a transverse **Hall voltage** $V_H$ appears across the faces perpendicular to both.

Derivation: the magnetic force $qv_dB$ piles charge on one face until the Hall field balances it, $qE_H=qv_dB$, with $J=nqv_d$:
$$E_H=\frac{JB}{nq},\quad R_H=\frac{E_H}{JB}=\frac{1}{nq},\quad V_H=\frac{IB}{nqt}=\frac{R_HIB}{t}$$
($t$ = dimension **along $B$**; width does not appear.)

- Sign: $R_H<0$ for electrons (n-type), $R_H>0$ for holes (p-type).
- Mobility $\mu=\sigma|R_H|$; Hall angle $\tan\theta_H=\mu B$.
- Uses: type and density of carriers, mobility, measuring $B$ (Hall probe), current sensors.
subtopics.basics_md: A magnet sideways pushes moving charges to one edge. The pile-up makes a voltage across the strip that grows with the field and shrinks with the number of carriers.
key_points: Setup: $I\perp B$, transverse $V_H$ across the third direction
Sign of $R_H$ gives carrier type (negative n-type, positive p-type)
$\mu=\sigma|R_H|$, $\tan\theta_H=\mu B$; applications: carrier type, density, mobility, B-meter

subtopics.title: Hall effect numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
All Hall numericals use one formula and unit care:
$$V_H=\frac{IB}{net}\ \Rightarrow\ n=\frac{IB}{eV_Ht},\qquad R_H=\frac{1}{ne},\qquad V_H=E_Hw=\frac{JBw}{ne}$$
- $t$ is the dimension along $B$; if only one dimension is given use it.
- **Convert**: gauss $\to$ tesla ($1\ \mathrm T=10^4$ G, so 2000 G $=0.2$ T); mm $\to$ m; mA $\to$ A; mV $\to$ V.
- $e=1.6\times10^{-19}$ C.
- Link to transport: $J=\sigma E=ne\mu E$, $\mu=\sigma|R_H|=|R_H|/\rho$.
- Free-electron metals: $n=$ (atoms per cell)$\times$(electrons per atom)$/a^3$; bcc has 2 atoms per cell.

subtopics.title: The p-n junction and its bias
subtopics.theory_md:
Where p and n meet, electrons and holes diffuse across and leave fixed ions: the **depletion region**, with a built-in field and **barrier potential**
$$V_0=\frac{k_BT}{e}\ln\frac{N_AN_D}{n_i^2}$$
(about 0.3 V Ge, 0.7 V Si).
- **Forward bias** (p to +): barrier falls, depletion narrows, current rises exponentially.
- **Reverse bias**: barrier rises, depletion widens, only a tiny reverse saturation current (minority carriers) flows.

Diode equation: $I=I_0\left(e^{eV/k_BT}-1\right)$.
subtopics.basics_md: Carriers leak across the border until the ions left behind build a hill that stops further crossing. Forward bias flattens the hill; reverse bias raises it.
key_points: Depletion region and barrier potential ($V_0\approx0.3$ V Ge, 0.7 V Si)
Forward bias narrows the depletion layer; reverse widens it

questions.q: The barrier potential of silicon is about
Explain the formation of the depletion layer and the barrier potential in a p-n junction.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Electrons diffuse from n to p, holes from p to n, and recombine near the junction.
2. This leaves **uncovered donor ions (+)** on the n side and **acceptor ions (-)** on the p side: the **depletion region**, free of mobile carriers.
3. The ions create a built-in field from n to p that opposes further diffusion.
4. Equilibrium is reached when the drift current balances the diffusion current; the potential difference across the layer is the **barrier potential** $V_0=\frac{kT}{e}\ln\frac{N_AN_D}{n_i^2}$ (0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge).

subtopics.title: Transistor structure and action
subtopics.theory_md:
A bipolar junction transistor has three doped regions: **emitter** (heavily doped, emits carriers), **base** (very thin, lightly doped), **collector** (wider, collects). Two types: n-p-n and p-n-p.

**Active region**: emitter-base **forward** biased, collector-base **reverse** biased. Emitter injects carriers into the base; because the base is thin and lightly doped, only about 1 to 5% recombine (base current) and the rest reach the collector.
$$I_E=I_B+I_C$$
In n-p-n the main carriers are electrons, in p-n-p holes. Other modes: cut-off (both junctions reverse) and saturation (both forward).
subtopics.basics_md: The emitter throws carriers at a very thin base; almost all fly through to the collector's strong pull, and a few get caught and form the small base current.
key_points: Emitter heavily doped, base thin and lightly doped, collector large
Active region: EB forward, CB reverse
Cut-off: both reverse; saturation: both forward

subtopics.title: CB, CE and CC configurations
subtopics.theory_md:
The same transistor can be wired with the base, emitter or collector as the common terminal.

| | CB | CE | CC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input / output | E-B / C-B | B-E / C-E | B-C / E-C |
| Current gain | $\alpha=I_C/I_E<1$ | $\beta=I_C/I_B$ (20-500) | $\gamma=I_E/I_B$ |
| Input resistance | low | medium | high |
| Output resistance | high | medium | low |
| Phase shift | 0 | 180 degrees | 0 |

CE is the usual amplifier (large current and voltage gain); CC (emitter follower) is used for impedance matching; CB for high-frequency use.
subtopics.basics_md: Which terminal is shared decides what is the input and what is the output, and so how big the gains and resistances turn out.
key_points: CC has highest input resistance and lowest output resistance

subtopics.title: Current gains alpha, beta, gamma and their relations
subtopics.theory_md:
$$\alpha=\frac{I_C}{I_E}\ (\text{CB}),\qquad \beta=\frac{I_C}{I_B}\ (\text{CE}),\qquad \gamma=\frac{I_E}{I_B}\ (\text{CC})$$
with $I_E=I_B+I_C$. Divide by $I_E$: $1=\dfrac{I_B}{I_E}+\alpha$, so $\dfrac{I_B}{I_E}=1-\alpha$. Then
$$\beta=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha},\quad \alpha=\frac{\beta}{1+\beta},\quad \gamma=\frac{I_E}{I_B}=1+\beta=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$$
Typical $\alpha$ = 0.95 to 0.99, $\beta$ = 20 to 500.
subtopics.basics_md: Everything follows from one fact: the emitter current splits into collector and base current. Dividing by the right current gives each gain.

subtopics.title: Leakage current and transistor numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
The collector junction is reverse biased, so a small **reverse saturation (leakage) current** $I_{CBO}$ flows with the emitter open.
- **CB**: $I_C=\alpha I_E+I_{CBO}$, and $I_B=I_E-I_C$.
- **CE**: $I_C=\beta I_B+(1+\beta)I_{CBO}$, with $I_{CEO}=(1+\beta)I_{CBO}$.
- $I_E=I_B+I_C$ always.

Steps: write the given values in the same unit (mA or $\mu$A), choose the CB or CE formula, then use $I_E=I_B+I_C$. In CE the leakage is amplified by $(1+\beta)$.
subtopics.basics_md: The leakage current rides on top of the useful current. In CE it is multiplied up, which is why it matters for biasing.

subtopics.title: Dynamic resistances and voltage gain
subtopics.theory_md:
In CE:
- **Input resistance** $r_i=\dfrac{\Delta V_{BE}}{\Delta I_B}$ at constant $V_{CE}$.
- **Output resistance** $r_o=\dfrac{\Delta V_{CE}}{\Delta I_C}$ at constant $I_B$.
- **Current gain** $\beta=\dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B}$.
- **Voltage gain** $A_v=\dfrac{\Delta V_{out}}{\Delta V_{in}}=\beta\dfrac{R_L}{r_i}$, **power gain** $=A_v\times\beta=\beta^2\dfrac{R_L}{r_i}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Gain in voltage is gain in current times the ratio of the load to the input resistance.
key_points: $r_i=\Delta V_{BE}/\Delta I_B$ and $r_o=\Delta V_{CE}/\Delta I_C$ from characteristics

subtopics.title: Photocell
subtopics.theory_md:
A **photocell** converts light into an electric current by the **photoelectric effect**.

Photoemissive type: an evacuated glass tube with a photosensitive cathode (Cs, K) and a positive anode. Light with $h\nu>\phi$ ejects electrons; the anode collects them, giving a **photocurrent proportional to intensity**.
$$h\nu=\phi+\tfrac12mv_{max}^2=\phi+eV_s,\quad \lambda_0=\frac{hc}{\phi}$$
(use $hc=1240$ eV nm.) Semiconductor types: **photoconductive** (LDR; light creates pairs so resistance falls) and **photovoltaic** (junction, EMF directly).

Uses: automatic doors, burglar alarms, light meters, street-light control.
subtopics.basics_md: A photon knocks out an electron only if it carries enough energy. Brighter light knocks out more electrons, which means more current, not faster electrons.
key_points: Cathode emits, anode collects, current $\propto$ intensity

subtopics.title: Solar cell
subtopics.theory_md:
A **solar cell** is a p-n junction with no external bias that turns sunlight into electrical power.

Principle: photons with $h\nu\ge E_g$ create electron-hole pairs in and near the depletion region; the **built-in field** sweeps electrons to n and holes to p, so a photovoltage appears and current flows through an external load. Si cell: $V_{oc}\approx0.5$ to 0.6 V, so cells are put in series for higher voltage and in parallel for current.

$$FF=\frac{V_mI_m}{V_{oc}I_{sc}},\qquad \eta=\frac{V_mI_m}{P_{in}}=\frac{FF\,V_{oc}I_{sc}}{P_{in}}$$
Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc}$, short-circuit current $I_{sc}$, maximum power point $(V_m,I_m)$.
subtopics.basics_md: Light makes pairs and the junction's own field pulls them apart; that separation is the cell's battery.
key_points: p-n junction, no bias; photons with $h\nu\ge E_g$ make pairs
Built-in field separates carriers, giving $V_{oc}$ and $I_{sc}$
Cells in series for voltage (one Si cell about 0.5 V)
